newsitem.title: CONGO: Caution and curiosity as Brazzaville awakes.
newsitem.headline: Caution and curiosity as Brazzaville awakes.

text.p: Cautious but curious, they emerge from their homes down side streets in Poto Poto -- a once vibrant corner of the Congo capital Brazzaville with its brightly painted shop, bar and restaurant signs.
At the main roundabout, the twisted bodies of a dozen victims of eight days of ethnic and political bloodshed lie where they fell, their faces distorted by decomposition.
Among the survivors, there are words of comfort for those grieving for lost loved ones.

Neighbours exchange greetings. Many have not seen one another since the bloody standoff between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso began on June 5.

"This is the first day we have come out of our homes at all," Kabuya Gregoire, a middle-aged resident, told journalists travelling with French soldiers on an evacuation mission on Friday. "It's been quiet since last night."
"Negotiations have started, haven't they?" asks Antoinette Bangula, a shopkeeper emerging from her home. "We hope it's going to be peaceful now."
Her shop, like others on the main street, has been looted.
The lull, which followed ceasefire calls on Wednesday by both Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso, brought hope.
It was too early to say a real truce had taken hold.
The fighting began after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.
The death toll is unknown. Aid workers and others have yet to reach many of the worst-hit areas.
French soldiers went to Poto Poto, which is under the control of Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia, to bring out three Togolese nationals and two half-French half-Togolese residents.
They were a small unit about 15 men in two light armoured vehicles.
Beer-drinking militiamen slouch or loll on street corners. Dressed in T-shirts and jeans, they carry AK-47 automatic rifles -- the status symbol of rebels or militiamen across Africa.
They threaten the visiting journalists -- idly it seems -- telling them they are not welcome and will be killed if they don't leave immediately.

"They (the fighters) say they are here to ensure security but when the bullets are whistling what kind of security is that for anyone?" said one Togolese woman, who declined to give her name. "Some of them say they are Cobras but really they are just thieves who join in to loot."
Witnesses say there has been fighting in the streets of Poto Poto every day since June 5. Every 50 to 100 metres (yards) lies an abandoned body -- mostly covered with cloth, all swarming with flies.
Isolated shots still ring out. South towards the city centre, the occasional rocket-propelled grenade can be heard.
French soldiers, over 1,200 foreign legionnaires and marine paratroops, have so far evacuated more than 3,400 foreign civilians.
For those left behind, the effect must have been strange but there was always hope...or humour.
"When are you coming for us?" more than one onlooker shouted as the French soldiers drove past.
